title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
tagline: The hydroxyl group, the acidity of phenol and the Williamson route to ethers.

overview.intro: Three families share the oxygen atom but differ completely in what that oxygen does. Alcohols are neutral to mildly basic and lose a proton only with difficulty, phenols are acidic enough to react with sodium hydroxide because the phenoxide charge delocalises into the ring, and ethers are almost inert because their C–O bonds are strong and unreactive. The chapter covers preparation of each family, the reactions that distinguish them, and the laboratory tests — the ferric chloride colour for phenol, the Lucas test for alcohols, the iodoform test for methyl carbinols — that the practical examination expects you to name and interpret.

facts.label: Classification
facts.value: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by the carbon bearing the –OH group.

facts.label: Acidity
facts.value: Phenol reacts with NaOH; alcohols do not. Both react with sodium metal.

facts.label: Tests
facts.value: Lucas distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3°; neutral FeCl3 gives violet with phenol; iodoform for CH3CH(OH)–.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Preparation, distinguishing tests and the dehydration order carry the marks.

learningOutcomes: Describe the preparation of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols and phenol by named methods.
Explain the acidic character of phenol compared with alcohols using resonance stabilisation.
Write the reactions of alcohols with sodium, hydrogen halides, oxidation agents and dehydration catalysts.
Distinguish between alcohols, phenols and ethers using named chemical tests.
Prepare ethers by the Williamson synthesis and explain why symmetrical ethers suit the method best.

blocks.text: Alcohols carry the hydroxyl group on an sp^3 carbon and are classified by how many carbons surround it, which in turn decides how they react. They are prepared by hydrating alkenes, by reducing carbonyl compounds, by hydrolysing halides and by the Grignard reaction with carbonyls, each method giving a different substitution pattern. Their reactions follow from the two bonds at oxygen: the O–H bond is weakly polar so alcohols react with sodium to release hydrogen, while the C–O bond breaks in substitution with hydrogen halides and in dehydration. Oxidation distinguishes the classes cleanly — primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids, secondary to ketones, and tertiary resist oxidation because no hydrogen remains on the carbinol carbon. Dehydration follows the orientation that gives the more substituted alkene, which is Saytzeff’s rule, and the ease of dehydration follows the same carbocation stability order as SN1: tertiary fastest, primary slowest.

items: Reaction with sodium: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H2, the hydrogen test for an –OH group.
With Lucas reagent, concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl2: tertiary alcohols turn cloudy at once, secondary in five minutes, primary only on heating.
Oxidation: primary → aldehyde → acid with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4; secondary → ketone; tertiary → no reaction.
Dehydration with concentrated H2SO4: 170 °C for ethanol to ethene, 140 °C giving diethyl ether instead.
Esterification with a carboxylic acid and concentrated sulphuric acid gives a sweet-smelling ester.
Saytzeff orientation gives the more substituted, more stable alkene as the major product.

items.note: The orange solution turns green as propanone forms, a positive secondary-alcohol result.
Immediate turbidity because the tertiary carbocation forms at once.

blocks.text: Phenol is a hydroxyl group bonded directly to an aromatic ring, and that arrangement changes everything. The oxygen lone pair overlaps with the ring’s pi system, so the ring becomes electron-rich and undergoes substitution far more readily than benzene, while the O–H bond becomes polar enough for phenol to react with sodium hydroxide — something an alcohol cannot do. Acidity is explained by the phenoxide ion: its negative charge delocalises into the ring at the ortho and para positions, spreading the charge and stabilising the anion, whereas the alkoxide of an alcohol has nowhere to delocalise. Phenol is prepared industrially by the cumene process, which oxidises cumene to a hydroperoxide and cleaves it to phenol and acetone in one useful step. Its reactions include bromination in water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate, the test for phenol; nitration with dilute acid to give nitrophenols; and the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, which introduces an aldehyde group using chloroform and alkali.

items: Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol; phenol turns blue litmus faintly but does not release hydrogen with sodium carbonate.
Phenol reacts with NaOH to give sodium phenoxide but not with sodium carbonate, distinguishing it from carboxylic acids.
Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, decolourising the bromine — the standard test.
Neutral ferric chloride gives a violet colour with phenol.
Reimer–Tiemann reaction gives salicylaldehyde using CHCl3 and NaOH.
Kolbe’s reaction gives salicylic acid by passing carbon dioxide into sodium phenoxide.

items.note: Immediate white precipitate and loss of the bromine colour, showing how strongly the ring is activated.
A violet complex confirms the enolic hydroxyl group.

items.meaning: Conjugate base of phenol, stabilised by delocalisation into the ring.
Industrial route to phenol from benzene via isopropylbenzene oxidation.
Formylation of phenol using chloroform and alkali to give salicylaldehyde.
Carboxylation of sodium phenoxide to salicylic acid.

learn.title: Ethers: preparation and the Williamson synthesis

blocks.text: Ethers have an oxygen bonded to two alkyl groups and are almost unreactive: the C–O bonds are strong, there is no O–H group to ionise, and no π bond to attack, so ethers serve as inert solvents and anaesthetics. Laboratory preparation passes an alcohol over heated alumina, or treats an alkoxide with an alkyl halide — the Williamson synthesis, an SN2 reaction between a phenoxide or alkoxide and a primary halide. The choice of partner matters: because the reaction is SN2, the halide must be unhindered, so a symmetrical ether comes from the appropriate pair while an unsymmetrical ether needs the alkyl group on the halide to be the less substituted one. Acidity explains a further difference in the Williamson route with phenol: phenol can be converted to phenoxide with sodium hydroxide, but an alcohol cannot, so phenolic ethers are made by reacting phenoxide with an alkyl halide rather than alcohol with base.

items: Laboratory method: heating the alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 at 140 °C gives a symmetrical ether.
Williamson: RONa + R′X → ROR′ + NaX by an SN2 attack of alkoxide on the halide.
Use a primary halide; a tertiary halide gives elimination instead of substitution.
Ethers are low boiling for their mass because they cannot hydrogen bond to themselves.
Diethyl ether was used as an anaesthetic and is still the common laboratory solvent for Grignard reactions.
Ethers form explosive peroxides on prolonged storage in air, which is why they are tested before distillation.

items.note: CH3CH2ONa + CH3CH2Br → CH3CH2OCH2CH3 + NaBr, giving diethyl ether in good yield.
The phenoxide nucleophile displaces iodide to give methoxybenzene, an anisole.

blocks.caption: Williamson synthesis: choosing the partners
rows: use sodium tert-butoxide with bromoethane instead

learn.title: Distinguishing the three families and the common tests

blocks.text: The practical course expects a student to take three unknown colourless liquids and place them, and each family has a reaction the others lack. Sodium metal reacts with alcohols and phenols to give hydrogen but not with ethers, immediately splitting off the inert family. Sodium hydroxide then separates the two hydroxyl compounds: phenol dissolves because its conjugate base is resonance-stabilised while an alcohol does not. Finally the alcohol classes separate among themselves by the Lucas test, and phenol confirms with a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride or a white precipitate with bromine water. The methyl carbinol test adds one more distinction: compounds containing the CH3CH(OH)– grouping give a yellow precipitate of iodoform with alkaline iodine, which is why ethanol gives the test but methanol does not. Knowing which observation belongs to which functional group converts an unknown into an identification.

items: Sodium: effervescence means –OH present, no reaction means ether.
NaOH: dissolution means phenol, no change means alcohol.
Lucas reagent: immediate cloudiness 3°, five minutes 2°, no change cold 1°.
Neutral FeCl3: violet colour confirms phenol.
Bromine water: white precipitate with phenol, decolourisation with an unsaturated compound.
Iodoform test: yellow precipitate with CH3CH(OH)– or CH3CO– compounds.

items.text: Ethanol gives a positive iodoform test
items.note: It contains the CH3CH(OH)– grouping and yields yellow CHI3 on warming with alkaline iodine.
It lacks the methyl carbinol grouping needed for the reaction.

keyPoints: Alcohols are classified primary, secondary and tertiary by the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group.
Reaction with sodium releases hydrogen and identifies an –OH group.
Oxidation gives aldehydes then acids from primary alcohols, ketones from secondary, nothing from tertiary.
Lucas reagent separates the three classes by the speed of cloudiness.
Dehydration follows Saytzeff orientation and is fastest for tertiary alcohols.
Phenol is acidic because the phenoxide charge delocalises into the ring.
Phenol reacts with NaOH but not with sodium carbonate, distinguishing it from carboxylic acids.
Bromine water gives a white precipitate with phenol; neutral ferric chloride gives violet.
Ethers are inert and prepared by the Williamson SN2 reaction using a primary halide.
The iodoform test identifies CH3CH(OH)– and CH3CO– groupings by a yellow precipitate.
examFocus: Distinguishing questions want a sequence: reagent, observation, conclusion — write all three.
Explain phenol acidity with the resonance structures of phenoxide, not with the word delocalisation alone.
Williamson answers must name the halide class; a tertiary halide gives elimination and loses marks.
Give the temperature in dehydration equations because 140 °C and 170 °C give different products.

vocabulary.meaning: –OH bonded to carbon, defining the alcohols and phenols.
The carbon atom carrying the hydroxyl group in an alcohol.
Concentrated hydrochloric acid with anhydrous zinc chloride, used to classify alcohols.
Elimination favours the more substituted, more stable alkene.
The resonance-stabilised conjugate base of phenol.
Test giving yellow CHI3 with methyl carbinol or methyl ketone groupings.
Ether formation by SN2 reaction of an alkoxide with a primary halide.
Elimination of water from an alcohol to give an alkene or ether.
Formylation of phenol with chloroform and alkali to give salicylaldehyde.
Reversible reaction of an acid with an alcohol giving an ester and water.

questions.prompt: Which compound reacts with sodium hydroxide solution but an alcohol does not?
questions.explanation: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised, so phenol is acidic enough to dissolve in alkali; alkoxides are not.

questions.prompt: The Lucas reagent turns cloudy immediately with:
questions.explanation: The tertiary alcohol forms a carbocation at once, so the insoluble alkyl chloride separates immediately.

questions.prompt: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate gives:
questions.explanation: With one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon the alcohol oxidises to a carbonyl and stops there.

questions.prompt: The Williamson synthesis of an unsymmetrical ether fails when it uses:
options: A primary alkyl halide and an alkoxide
A tertiary alkyl halide and an alkoxide
A phenoxide and a methyl halide
questions.answer: A tertiary alkyl halide and an alkoxide
questions.explanation: The reaction is SN2, and a tertiary halide undergoes elimination with the alkoxide instead of substitution.

questions.prompt: The yellow precipitate formed by a compound containing the CH3CH(OH) group on warming with alkaline iodine is called iodo __________ .
questions.explanation: The iodoform test identifies methyl carbinols and methyl ketones by this characteristic precipitate.

questions.prompt: The rule stating that elimination favours the more substituted alkene is known as Saytzeff’s __________ .
questions.explanation: The more substituted alkene is more stable, so it forms in greater amount when more than one product is possible.

questions.prompt: Explain why phenol is acidic while ethanol is not.
questions.answer: When phenol loses a proton the negative charge on the phenoxide oxygen overlaps with the ring pi system and delocalises to the ortho and para positions, spreading the charge over five atoms and stabilising the anion. In ethanol the ethoxide ion has no such delocalisation, so the charge stays on one oxygen and the alkoxide is far less stable, making the alcohol effectively neutral to aqueous alkali.
questions.explanation: Acidity depends on the stability of the conjugate base; resonance stabilisation exists only in phenol.

questions.prompt: Give two chemical tests that distinguish phenol from an alcohol and state the observation for each.
questions.answer: First, sodium hydroxide solution: phenol dissolves to give a clear solution of sodium phenoxide while an alcohol does not react. Second, neutral ferric chloride solution: phenol gives a violet colour while an alcohol gives no colour change. Bromine water is an alternative, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol with phenol only.
questions.explanation: Both tests rely on properties unique to the phenolic hydroxyl group.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of diethyl ether from ethanol and explain why the temperature must be carefully controlled.
questions.answer: Ethanol is mixed with concentrated sulphuric acid and the mixture is heated. At 140 °C one molecule of ethanol is protonated by the acid and a second, acting as a nucleophile, displaces water from it in an SN2 step, giving diethyl ether. Temperature control is essential because the same reagents at 170 °C favour elimination: protonated ethanol loses water to give ethene instead, and at still higher temperatures oxidation and charring occur. The ether is then distilled off as it forms, which also helps to keep the equilibrium moving towards the product.
questions.explanation: Intermolecular substitution dominates near 140 °C while intramolecular elimination dominates near 170 °C.

questions.prompt: An organic compound C3H8O dissolves in sodium metal but not in sodium hydroxide, gives a positive iodoform test and oxidises to a ketone. Identify it and justify each observation.
questions.answer: The compound is propan-2-ol. It reacts with sodium because it contains a hydroxyl group, releasing hydrogen. It fails with sodium hydroxide because it is an aliphatic alcohol whose alkoxide is not resonance-stabilised, so no acidity is shown towards alkali. It gives a positive iodoform test because it carries the CH3CH(OH)– grouping, which is oxidised to a methyl ketone and then halogenated to give yellow CHI3. Oxidation gives propanone, a ketone, which identifies it as a secondary alcohol rather than propan-1-ol.
questions.explanation: Every observation is consistent only with the secondary alcohol bearing a methyl carbinol group.
